item.dc:creator: vmwareblogs

item.content:encoded:
If you have ever watched an infrastructure engineer tab between a dozen dashboards at 2 AM trying to track down a latency issue causing application problems, then you already understand the problem. Infrastructure management has long operated in a mouse-click-driven world. That is changing fast.

In a new MonkCast video podcast, analyst Rachel Stephens of RedMonk discussed with me how VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 9.1 is evolving day-two operations from static information toward programmable, API-driven workflows with real-time observability.

Watch a 90-second excerpt on YouTube Shorts

Watch the full episode on YouTube

Want the key takeaways before you tune in? Here is how VCF 9.1 is reshaping private cloud programmability:

VCF 9.1 expands the VCF API surface with access to real-time platform data.

The new fleet management capabilities in VCF Operations simplify scaling compute, storage, and networking infrastructure. 

Teams can execute tasks centrally across the entire infrastructure stack using APIs, ensuring consistency and eliminating manual maintenance at scale. 

VCF Operations can collect metrics down to 2-second intervals. These 2-second metrics are designed for programmatic consumption. Native Prometheus compatibility and PromQL support allow automated scripts to detect micro-anomalies instantly. 

Log formats historically varied across infrastructure components. VCF 9.1 standardizes log schemas across the stack, making it seamless to pipe logs directly into tools like Kafka, Slack, or AI pipelines. 

VCF 9.1 replaces risky, long-lived service account passwords with native OAuth 2.0 support. Users and API scripts exchange standard OAuth tokens for short-lived bearer tokens, limiting access duration and minimizing the blast radius of leaked credentials.

If you are trying to run a private cloud at scale, you will come away with a clear picture of where operations programmability is heading.

You can start building these programmable workflows today. VCF Operations gives you visibility across the entire private cloud, and SDKs are available in Python and Java. Watch the MonkCast episode with Rachel Stephens to see the details, and then explore the VCF Operations APIs and SDKs to try it for yourself. Also read this blog about programmability in VCF 9.1.

item.content:encoded:
Kubernetes doesn’t have to require a separate team, a separate security policy, a separate management plane, and a separate budget. The status quo for most enterprises is that Kubernetes infrastructure exists in a silo alongside the VM-based infrastructure that still runs the majority of production workloads. That duplication is expensive and operationally complex. It’s also becoming unsustainable as AI workloads, which often need both containerized services and persistent VM-based infrastructure, blur the line between the two worlds.

VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) addresses this with VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS), a CNCF-certified Kubernetes runtime built directly into VCF, enabling organizations to run containers and VMs on a single unified private cloud platform. The VCF platform includes three core services for app modernization: VKS, Container Service, and VM Service. These services share one control plane, one policy model, and one operational experience across every workload you run. At VMware Explore 2026, we have over 50 featured sessions covering every angle of how these services work individually and together.

Whether you are modernizing your first VM workload or operating thousands of containers at scale, you will find answers to the questions your team is wrestling with right now:

  • Not sure which deployment model fits your apps? A dedicated breakout session (CLOB1236LV) compares VM Service, Container Service, and VKS side by side with real-world scenarios, a common UI and API walkthrough, and decision criteria to match the right model to your applications. 
  • Running VMs today and want to modernize without disruption? A new breakout session (CLOB1455LV) this year demystifies VM Service, showing how it delivers real vSphere VMs with full vMotion, DRS, and HA support through a streamlined modern provisioning model, including Day 2 tasks like snapshots, resizing, and migrations. 
  • Developers asking for more speed without Ops losing control? In session APPB1222LV, see how Container Service and VKS together take an app from code commit to running cluster in under 10 minutes, with CI/CD, GitOps, and integrated observability built-in.
  • Scaling AI workloads on private infrastructure? VKS runs AI workloads on VCF, from GPU-accelerated training clusters to real-time medical imaging inference. Sponsor session CLOQT1892LVS demonstrates how radiology AI models can be deployed on VKS and run at sub-second latency within the hospital data center.
  • Security is your first question? The People’s Choice Award winner breakout session SECB1079LV covers Zero Trust enforcement across multi-cluster VKS with microsegmentation, mTLS, WAF, and automated policy rollouts in a single workflow. 
  • Want proof before you commit? Broadcom runs thousands of containers at scale daily on VKS and shares exactly how in a session [CLOB1286LV] open to everyone. Hear directly from enterprise IT leaders on TCO savings, platform consolidation, and operational wins.
  • Hands-on learner? Expert-led and self-paced labs let you dive deep into VKS, benchmark performance, configure VKS security with vDefend and Avi, and explore VCF lifecycle operations.

Across breakouts, tutorials, hands-on labs, quick talks, expert roundtables, and theater sessions, Explore 2026 covers everything from your first Kubernetes cluster to Zero Trust security, Private AI, edge deployments, and live customer stories. Whatever your role or starting point, there’s a session designed for your next step.

Browse the full session list here.

item.content:encoded:
Enterprise infrastructure teams face a brutal cost environment in 2026. Server prices are skyrocketing. Hardware supply chains remain constrained. Teams are running denser, more demanding workloads like AI inference, GPU pipelines, and large in-memory databases. Memory costs, specifically DRAM, have become one of the single largest line items in infrastructure procurement. Storage capacity is also growing more expensive. And on top of all of this, AI workloads are pushing resource consumption higher than earlier capacity planning models anticipated.

AI investments are eating into IT budgets, often displacing infrastructure investments and forcing teams to do more with less. Simply buying more hardware is no longer a viable response. Instead, the organizations winning this fight are using software intelligence to get far more value from the infrastructure they already own.

Take DRAM, for example. It has become the most cost-sensitive component in modern servers, driven by the insatiable memory appetites of high-density workloads. NVMe memory tiering in VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) addresses this directly. By intelligently distinguishing between “hot” memory (actively accessed pages that require DRAM speed) and “cold” memory (infrequently accessed pages that tolerate slightly higher latency), NVMe memory tiering dramatically reduces DRAM requirements and lowers TCO by up to 40%.

Storage efficiency represents another major optimization opportunity that many organizations have yet to fully capture. Storage advances, such as global deduplication and next-generation compression algorithms, are now native to VCF via vSAN, creating new opportunities to reduce your storage TCO by up to 39% versus external, controller-based arrays.

At VMware Explore 2026 in Las Vegas, we’ll share all the ways that VCF can help you wring every last resource out of your servers. We’ll introduce you to NVMe memory tiering; VMware vSAN global deduplication, which enables up to 8x reduction in used capacity; and vSAN’s enhanced compression. We will also demonstrate how to reduce memory requirements for vSAN ReadyNodes by up to 67%, and explain how to repurpose older servers with VMware Cloud Foundation 9.0 and later. You’ll leave the event equipped to navigate the hardware supply crunch with confidence.

The following sessions will focus on managing and lowering hardware costs:

Conquer the 2026 Hardware Crisis: VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1 Optimization Strategies [CLOB1266LV]

Avoiding the RAM-pocalypse: Unlock Total Cost of Ownership Savings with VMware Memory Tiering [CLOB1046LV]

Beat the Hardware Supply Crisis with VMware Cloud Foundation [VBT2025LV]

Save your seats now and take advantage of all that Explore 2026 has to offer.

Thank you to Tom Nagelmeyer and Harshad Kolte for contributing to this article.

item.title: Operationalizing VMware Cloud Foundation Control Plane for Kubernetes Workloads
item.dc:creator: vmwareblogs
item.description:
In today’s fast-evolving IT landscape, enterprise IT organizations face a fundamental operational dilemma. On one side, VMware vSphere and infrastructure administrators require strict control, compliance, security, and multi-tenant resource governance. The post Operationalizing VMware Cloud Foundation Control Plane for  Kubernetes Workloads appeared first on VMware Blogs.
item.content:encoded:
In today’s fast-evolving IT landscape, enterprise IT organizations face a fundamental operational dilemma. On one side, VMware vSphere and infrastructure administrators require strict control, compliance, security, and multi-tenant resource governance. On the other side, developers and DevOps engineers need agility, rapid self-service provisioning, and native API-driven infrastructure to accelerate application delivery. 

When these two priorities collide, operational friction is inevitable. Infrastructure teams become overwhelmed by endless ticket queues for cluster provisioning and network changes, while development teams, frustrated by delays, turn to shadow IT or deploy siloed external management clusters. This fragmentation not only slows down innovation but also introduces significant security vulnerabilities, operational overhead, and cost inefficiencies. 

In our recent webinar, Activating VKS Supervisor to Support Kubernetes, we demonstrated how activating the control plan, referred to as the vSphere Supervisor, in VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 9.1 directly resolves this modern app dilemma. 

VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) is the Kubernetes runtime built natively in VCF. With CNCF-certified Kubernetes, VKS enables platform engineers to deploy, manage, and scale Kubernetes clusters while leveraging a comprehensive set of cloud services in VCF, as well as all conformant third-party services. 

Bridging the Gap: What is the vSphere Supervisor?

Enterprise platform teams face a persistent operational tension: developers need rapid, self-service Kubernetes APIs, while infrastructure teams must enforce centralized governance, security, and resource compliance. 

The vSphere Supervisor resolves this friction by delivering true developer self-service backed by enterprise-grade administrative control, all running directly on your existing vSphere infrastructure. Instead of building and maintaining complex, siloed management clusters on top of vSphere, Supervisor integrates a native Kubernetes control plane directly into VMware ESXi and vSphere, converting hypervisors into native Kubernetes endpoints.

This architecture establishes a shared, multi-tenant platform where both infrastructure admins and developers operate harmoniously: 

  • For vSphere Admins: Control and compliance are preserved through vSphere Namespaces. Admins define resource boundaries (CPU, memory, storage quotas), assign role-based access control (RBAC), and maintain full operational visibility via the vSphere Client and VMware Cloud Foundation Operations. 
  • For DevOps Engineers: The platform presents a standard Kubernetes API endpoint. Engineers can consume declarative YAML manifests through kubectl and Helm to provision workload clusters (VKS clusters), virtual machines (via the VM Service), and containerized workloads directly within assigned vSphere Namespaces. 

In VCF 9.1, decoupled lifecycle management allows platform teams to patch and upgrade Kubernetes versions independently of underlying platform updates. Combined with major VKS engine optimizations, the platform delivers up to 70% faster cluster deployments, up to 75% faster upgrades, and scales up to 500 clusters per control plane instance.

vSphere Supervisor Architecture and High Availability

The vSphere Supervisor architecture is designed to deliver enterprise-grade resilience by embedding a native, high-availability Kubernetes control plane directly into the vSphere hypervisor layer. The vSphere Supervisor control plane consists of three active Kubernetes control plane virtual machines (VMs) deployed across ESX hosts or multi-zone vSphere clusters, ensuring continuous quorum and zero single points of failure. These control plane VMs collaborate directly with vCenter and ESX to manage workload lifecycles, resource allocations, and state reconciliation across the environment. Under the hood, storage and compute primitives are tightly coupled to guarantee high availability. The control plane placement algorithm dynamically handles VM placement across fault domains, while transient data is managed via Ephemeral Disks that automatically clean up upon pod termination. Additionally, container image disks are cached directly on individual ESX hosts, bypassing registry download latency to enable near-instantaneous pod creation and recovery during host failover events. 

Storage Topologies and Policy Management

Stateful, cloud-native applications require robust persistent storage handling. The vSphere Supervisor seamlessly connects Kubernetes persistent volume requests with vSphere storage primitives through Cloud Native Storage (CNS) and the native vSphere Container Storage Interface (CSI) driver. 

When a developer submits a Kubernetes PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC), the CNS-CSI driver interfaces directly with vCenter to translate the claim into a First Class Disk (FCD) on the underlying storage. Admins enforce governance by assigning storage policies (e.g., Gold, Silver) and capacity caps directly to vSphere Namespaces. 

The vSphere Supervisor supports three distinct storage topologies tailored to specific workload requirements:

While hyperconverged vSAN is commonly highlighted, traditional external storage arrays (Fibre Channel, iSCSI, and NFS) map directly into these same topologies. Standard external SAN/NAS datastores provisioned to a single vSphere cluster function as Zonal Datastores. In multi-zone deployments, customers utilizing third-party array replication, such as FC/iSCSI Metro Storage Clusters can achieve Cross-Zone Datastore availability without requiring a native vSAN Stretched Cluster.

Beyond persistent storage, vSphere Supervisor manages Control Plane Disks, Ephemeral Disks (automatically destroyed at pod teardown), and Container Image Caching directly on ESX hosts to enable near-instantaneous pod boot speeds. 

vSphere Supervisor Networking and Load Balancing

Networking and load balancing within vSphere Supervisor are engineered around a decoupled, highly scalable Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) model implemented through VMware NSX System Projects and Centralized Transit Gateways. Each vSphere Namespace operates within its own dedicated NSX VPC, complete with private subnets and VPC Gateways that isolate tenant workloads and eliminate IP address conflicts, even across teams using overlapping CIDR blocks. Traffic routing across namespaces, management networks, and external services is managed via Tier-0 and Tier-1 Transit Gateways, helping ensure secure, high-throughput network fabric transit. For load balancing and traffic ingress, vSphere Supervisor seamlessly integrates with VMware Avi Load Balancer. This integration automates the provisioning and lifecycle management of virtual IP addresses (VIPs), Kubernetes API endpoint load balancers, and L4/L7 ingress controllers, providing fine-grained traffic management, zero-touch network automation, and deep security isolation without requiring manual networking intervention. 

Modern Networking: NSX VPCs and Transit Gateways

Networking across multi-tenant container platforms has traditionally caused significant friction, often resulting in IP address exhaustion, firewall routing complexities, and security risks. 

The vSphere Supervisor solves this by pairing NSX Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs) with adaptable transit gateway designs in NSX System Projects. Although our webinar demo highlighted a Centralized Transit Gateway implementation, vSphere Supervisor fully supports Distributed Transit Gateways as well, allowing you to choose the connectivity model that best fits your environment.

Key capabilities of this networking framework include: 

  • Isolated VPCs per Namespace: Every vSphere Namespace is isolated inside its own NSX VPC, complete with private subnets and dedicated VPC Gateways. 
  • Zero IP Conflicts and Decoupled Routing: Decoupled routing across VPCs allows separate development teams to use overlapping IP ranges without network collisions. 
  • Linear Scalability: Centralized Transit Gateways handle high-throughput, cross-namespace, and external transit routing securely via Tier-0/Tier-1 gateways. 
  • Integrated Load Balancing: Avi Load Balancer automates ingress controller traffic routing and Kubernetes API load balancing seamlessly. 

Step-by-Step Activation and Demo Workflow
During the demonstration portion of our webinar, we walked through the complete end-to-end deployment lifecycle from both administrative and developer perspectives. 

Day-2 Observability: Full telemetry, performance metrics, and logs flow directly into centralized VCF Operations for proactive monitoring and lifecycle operations. 

Prerequisites and Activation Trigger: Before triggering the Supervisor activation, ensure the core prerequisites are met: an active VCF Workload Domain with vSphere HA and DRS enabled, an NSX or vSphere Distributed Switch network configuration with assigned IP pools, a supported load balancer, a dedicated vSphere storage policy, and a Subscribed Content Library. Activation can then be initiated during Workload Domain creation in VCF Operations or post-deployment directly in vCenter under Supervisor Management -> Get Started, where the wizard validates compute zones, storage policies, content libraries, and load balancing configurations before provisioning. 

Namespace and RBAC Configuration: The VI Admin creates a vSphere Namespace, assigns storage policies and resource quotas, and grants developer access rights. 

Declarative Provisioning: The DevOps engineer authenticates to the vSphere Supervisor control plane via kubectl and applies a YAML manifest to request a new VKS cluster. vSphere Supervisor automatically provisions control plane and worker nodes. 

Dual-Perspective Visibility: The VI Admin monitors infrastructure health and VM objects inside vSphere/VCF Operations, while the developer manages pods, services, and deployments using kubectl. 

Hybrid App Deployment: Teams deploy multi-tier applications combining virtual machines (via the VM Service API) and containerized workloads using Helm charts. 

Conclusion and What’s Next

Activating vSphere Supervisor transforms traditional enterprise virtualization into a powerful, multi-tenant cloud platform. By providing developers with native Kubernetes self-service while giving IT administrators total resource and governance control, VKS accelerates modern application delivery without increasing operational risk. 

To experience the full walkthrough step-by-step, make sure to check out the full webinar recording.

Ready to Get Hands-On?

  • Hands-on Labs: Try our Hands-on Lab with Kubernetes.
  • Official Documentation: Check out these resources.
    • Using Harbor as a Supervisor Service
    • Enabling VKS Management in an Air-Gapped Environment
    • Deploying Bitnami Harbor OVA for Air-Gapped VKS Deployments
  • Learning Courses: Log in to Learning@Broadcom via the Broadcom Support Portal, under the “Education Portal,” to access the following VKS courses.
    • VKS Configure and Consume
    • VKS Advanced Design
    • VKS Advanced Configuration
    • VKS Advanced Troubleshooting
    • VCAP VKS Certification 

Need assistance with your VKS projects? Contact your Broadcom Account Manager to learn how VCF Professional Services and Partners like TeraSky can help advance your initiatives.

Deploying a secure Kubernetes cluster on day one is hard enough. Keeping it secure, compliant, and resilient through every upgrade, scaling event, and lifecycle change is where most platform teams struggle. That gap between day-one deployment and day-two confidence is exactly what VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) 3.7 was built to close.

Welcome to the next episode of the VCF Breakroom Chats. Today, we are happy to present this vLog with Natalie Fisher, Principal Cloud Native Strategist and Ecosystem Lead. In this episode, Natalie Fisher and Jay Thontakudi discuss key benefits for Platform Teams in deploying VKS 3.7. They include:

  • Zero-trust platform hardening and audit readiness
  • Scale and resilience for mission-critical workloads with faster time to value
  • Future-proof investments in conformant third-party tools with predictable support via the new add-on management framework
  • Simplified operations with multiple Kubernetes version support

You’ll gain relevant insights whether you’re operating Kubernetes in finance, healthcare, telecommunications, utilities, or other key sectors. This episode covers the security, resilience, and ecosystem changes that matter most to your platform teams, cloud admins, and development teams.

Learn more about deploying and managing all modern applications on VKS:

  • Check out the blog Introducing VKS 3.7
  • Explore more resources on the VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service website  
  • Watch the full episode above at YouTube Video of Episode 93

This webinar series focuses on VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF). In this series, we share conversations with industry-recognized experts from Broadcom and with solution partners and customers. You’ll gain relevant insights whether you’re an IT practitioner, IT admin, cloud or platform architect, developer, DevOps, senior IT manager, IT executive, or AI/ML professional.

item.content:encoded:
Whether you want to explore new feature sets, dissect the architecture of our event infrastructure, or challenge your skills, here is your playbook for the Hands-on Labs at Explore this year.

REGISTER NOW

Written By: Kelly Smith, Product Marketing Engineer, VMware Hands-on Labs

As a virtual infrastructure or cloud administrator, you spend your days managing environments, keeping up with change, and evaluating where your private cloud strategy is heading next. The best way to master new capabilities isn’t watching a passive demo—it’s logging directly into a live console and driving the software yourself with expert guidance nearby.

That is why the Hands-on Labs room is the ultimate destination for technical administrators and engineers at Explore. This is where you get exclusive, first-look access to our brand-new VCF 9.1 lab content. While VCF 9.1 went GA earlier this summer, Explore is the official in-person debut of the lab environments built specifically around it.

1. The Heavy Hitters: 36 Expert-led Workshops

Think of our Expert-led Workshops as highly technical, interactive deep dives led directly by the specialists who live and breathe this technology in the field every day.

  • Admin Access: These workshops bypass passive observation and place you directly inside a live, fully-functioning sandbox environment with admin rights.
  • Direct Line to Field Experts: These 36 workshops are developed and presented by the actual Subject Matter Experts (SMEs) who built the labs. They work directly with customers in the field daily, giving you a direct line to ask practical, real-world questions about architecture, migration, automation, or security.
  • Deep Technical Variety: This year’s catalog covers the critical fronts of modern infrastructure management, including:
    • Core Cloud Operations: Day 2 diagnostics, health triage, and performance tuning (like vNUMA and processor optimization).
    • Advanced Networking & Storage: Multi-site BGP peering, native VPC routing, and advanced Elastic Storage Architecture (ESA).
    • Automation & Next-Gen Workloads: Infrastructure-as-code deployments with Salt, workload mobility with HCX, and even building your first Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) app with private AI.
  • The Standby Hack: Because these sessions offer such high-value technical depth, they fill up instantly in the catalog. If a workshop you need is marked as full, show up to the room anyway. Standby seats are available onsite for walk-in practitioners to cover last-minute no-shows.

2. Learn at Your Own Pace: Over 30 Self-paced Labs

Need to break away from a rigid schedule, or want to dive deep into a specific VCF 9.1 configuration on your own time?

  • 30+ Interactive Lab Titles: Our Self-paced Labs catalog features over 30 unique, interactive titles covering the entire portfolio. There is no pre-registration or scheduling required—just walk in, grab an open station, and start learning.
  • SMEs on Standby: Just because it’s a Self-paced Lab doesn’t mean you’re learning in isolation. Our product SMEs are stationed right on the floor. If you hit an interesting scenario, have a question about a new 9.1 feature, or want to know how a lab configuration translates to your real-world environment, just raise your hand.

3. Peak “Software on Software”: The Hands-on Labs Tour & Command Center

Ever wondered what it takes to spin up, monitor, and tear down thousands of highly concurrent, live nested lab environments for an event of this scale? We do it by running our own software stack at absolute peak capacity.

  • The 12-Screen Command Center Wall: See the real-time performance, compute, storage, and networking metrics of the entire Hands-on Labs event space in real time. This is a true, live showcase of the platform operating under extreme real-world pressure.
  • Go Behind the Scenes: Join our infrastructure admins, performance teams, and lab builders for the Hands-on Labs Tour of our deployment architecture. We’ll talk capacity planning, automation, and how we handle the massive workloads generated by thousands of concurrent users.
  • Deep Dive Ahead: Want a sneak peek at the infrastructure and business logic that powers this massive operation? Read our dedicated Hands-on Labs Tour blog post here for the full architectural breakdown.

4. Challenge Your Skills: Odyssey & The VCF Lab Explorer’s Tracker 

We know that technical admins love a friendly challenge and a bit of bragging rights. We have built-in opportunities to do both.

  • The Odyssey Tournament: Think you’re the fastest admin in the room? Put your troubleshooting and configuration skills to the test in our gamified live-lab tournament. Race against your peers to solve real-world technical challenges, climb the live leaderboard, and walk away with major prizes and ultimate bragging rights. Details on the challenge and prizes in this blog post.
  • VCF Lab Explorer Tracker: Start your journey by visiting the VCF demo booth on the show floor to grab your VCF Keychain. From there, head over to the Hands-on Labs area, complete specific technical milestones, and collect exclusive charms to add to your keychain. Completing your passport unlocks a custom plushie and enters you for a chance to win a highly coveted, limited-edition VCF sweatshirt.

Lock In Your Schedule

The Hands-on Labs room is where you stop watching demos and start actually using the new technology.

  • Browse the catalog and reserve your Expert-led Workshop seats now
  • Read our deep-dive on the Hands-on Labs Command Center
  • Learn more about the Hands-on Labs Tour
  • Get all the details on Odyssey rules, times, and prizes
REGISTER NOW

Stay connected with VMware Hands-on Labs on X, Facebook, and YouTube.

Are you a fan of hands-on learning? Check out this ultimate guide for Hands-on Labs at #VMwareExplore 2026 in Las Vegas!
